title: Consistency models: how up to date does a read have to be?
dek: Strong, eventual and the useful guarantees in between, what each costs, and how to choose one feature at a time: a rider's assignment, a menu price, a like count.

items: Once data has copies, a read can land on a copy that hasn't caught up. A consistency model is the promise about what a read may see.
Strong (linearizable): every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy. Needed for things only one person may have: a rider assignment, the last coupon, a username, a balance.
Eventual: copies agree if writes stop for a moment; until then a read may be old. Fine for menus, ratings, counts and search.
In between are the guarantees users notice: see your own changes, never go back in time, and see causes before effects. They're cheap and fix most complaints.
Choose per feature, not per system. Strong costs time on every request, and across regions it can mean refusing requests during a network split.

body.x: The C in ACID means a transaction never breaks the rules you set, such as a non-negative balance or a foreign key. Isolation, the I, is about transactions running at the same time on one database; the Databases article covers that with the last coupon. This article is about the other meaning: when the same data lives on several machines, how fresh is what a read returns?

An India match. People in the stadium see each ball as it's bowled. The TV feed is a few seconds behind, the score app a little more, and tomorrow's newspaper a day. They all end up agreeing on the result; what differs is how old the score is when you look.

body.cap: A restaurant changes a biryani from ₹250 to ₹280 at 100 ms. A strong read shows ₹280 from that moment, and so does the owner when their reads go to the leader after a change. A customer on a replica 250 ms behind sees the old price until 350 ms. A customer whose reads bounce between two replicas sees ₹280, then ₹250 again: time going backwards.

body.name: Strong
body.what: Once a write is confirmed, every read anywhere returns it or something newer. The system behaves as if there were one copy.
body.use: Anything only one person may have: assigning a rider, the last unit of stock or coupon, unique usernames, account balances, locks and leader election.
body.avoid: Reads that can be slightly old: you pay for strong on every request, and across regions each one waits for a round trip.
body.ex: Accepting order 123 with `UPDATE … WHERE rider_id IS NULL` on the leader.
body.like: One register on one desk: whoever writes in it first, everyone after sees it.

body.name: Causal
body.what: If one write depends on another, everyone sees them in that order. Unrelated writes may appear in any order.
body.use: Conversations and anything with replies: support chats, comments, a refund after its complaint.
body.avoid: Things needing one global winner, such as the last item in stock: causal order doesn't pick one.
body.ex: A customer's message and the agent's reply always appear in that order.
body.like: A WhatsApp group: you never see the answer before the question.

body.name: Session guarantees
body.what: Promises for one user's session: you see your own changes, and you never see older data than you already saw.
body.use: Almost every screen where a user edits something and looks again. These fix most "it didn't save" complaints.
body.avoid: Relying on them across users: another user may still see the old value.
body.ex: After a restaurant edits its menu, its own reads go to the leader for a minute; customers can lag.
body.like: Your own notebook: whatever you wrote, you see on the next page.

body.name: Eventual
body.what: If writes stop, all copies end up the same. Until then, any read may be old, and two reads may disagree.
body.use: Menus, photos, ratings, like and view counts, search results, recommendations, analytics.
body.avoid: Anything that must not be decided twice: two replicas can each say yes.
body.ex: The rating shown on a restaurant card, updated a few seconds after a review.
body.like: News spreading through a family WhatsApp: everyone hears, not at the same moment.

body.cap: Two riders tap Accept on order 123 a few milliseconds apart. If each replica decides, both see the order as free and both say yes. If one copy decides with a conditional write, only the first changes a row; the second changes nothing and the app tells the rider the order is taken.

items: Uniqueness: one username, one rider per order, the last unit of stock. Let one copy decide, with a unique index or a conditional write. The Contention concept has the patterns.
Money: balances and wallet top-ups go through the leader in a transaction. Read them from the leader too when the number matters.
Coordination: locks, leader election and configuration go in a store built for it (etcd, ZooKeeper, or the database's leader), not a cache.
Everything else can be weaker. Ask "what breaks if this read is two seconds old?" If the answer is "nothing much", it doesn't need strong.

body.x: Where eventual is fine, and how fine

"Eventually" needs a number. Say how stale is acceptable: the menu within 5 seconds, a rating within a minute, the analytics dashboard within an hour. That number decides the design: a cache TTL, how far replicas may lag before they're taken out, how often a search index refreshes.
Remember that caches and CDNs are copies too. A page served from a CDN with a 60-second TTL is eventually consistent, whatever the database behind it promises.

items: Single-leader databases: read from the leader for strong, from replicas for eventual. Read-your-writes is "leader for this user right after a change".
DynamoDB: reads are eventual by default; ask for a strongly consistent read and pay twice the read units, in one region.
Cassandra and other quorum stores: choose per query. `QUORUM` writes and reads give read-your-latest-write; `ONE` is fast and eventual.
Global strong consistency (Spanner, CockroachDB) works by having copies agree through consensus on every write, so writes take at least one round trip between regions.
Monotonic reads: keep each user on the same replica (by user ID), or carry the last version seen and wait for a replica that has it.

body.x: Isolation is consistency's cousin inside one database: what one transaction can see of others running at the same time. Most databases default to the middle.

body.label: Isolation levels
head: Level
Prevents
Still possible
Default in
rows: Two reads in one transaction disagree; lost updates
Write skew: two transactions each check, then both write
Nothing; some transactions are aborted and must retry

items: Strong costs latency: a read or write waits for the one copy that decides, and across regions that is tens of milliseconds or more.
Strong costs availability in a split: if a region is cut off from the copy that decides, it must refuse writes rather than risk two answers. The CAP article goes into this.
Eventual costs code: screens and support processes must cope with old data, and some bugs only appear under lag.
Mixing models costs clarity. Write down, per feature, which one it uses.
Don't say "we need strong consistency" for everything. Go feature by feature.
Name the strong ones and how: "rider assignment is a conditional update on the leader".
Give eventual a number: "menus can be 5 seconds stale; we cache for 5 seconds".
Mention read-your-writes for anyone editing their own data.
If there are several regions, say what happens to writes when one is cut off.

body.x: "The menu everyone reads" is a read-heavy challenge where a cache in front of the database is the answer, and the cache serves copies that can be a little old. Try it and decide how stale a menu may be.
